unesco.title: Cheoyongmu
unesco.description: Cheoyongmu is a court dance today performed on stage but formerly used to dispel evil spirits and pray for tranquillity at royal banquets or during exorcism rites on New Year’s Eve to promote good fortune. Based on the Korean legend of Cheoyong, a son of the dragon king Yongwang, who took human form and saved his human wife from the smallpox spirit through singing and dancing, the dance is performed by five men clad in white, blue, black, red and yellow to represent the four cardinal directions and the centre. They wear the light wine-coloured mask of the man-god, with white teeth, tin earrings with a necklace of lead beads, and a black hat decorated with two peony blossoms and seven peaches to ward off evil and invite auspicious energy. The dancers move with stateliness and vigour through a variety of styles and tempos of music, punctuated by various lyrical song recitations. Part of a greater folk mythology surrounding Cheoyong, including the belief that his image carved on the gate of a house would repel smallpox and other ills, Cheoyongmu also embodies the philosophy of Confucianism, particularly the Theory of the Five Elements. The creation of the Cheoyong masks also provides a valuable opportunity for traditional craftsmanship.

profile.name: Cheoyongmu
profile.tagline: A majestic five-person court dance from Korea designed to dispel evil spirits.
profile.insight: Danced by five men in masks of light wine-color, Cheoyongmu uses the philosophy of the Five Elements to transform a mythic exorcism of a smallpox spirit into a stately, vigorous performance of royal protection.
profile.profile: Cheoyongmu is the oldest surviving Korean court dance, originating from the Unified Silla period. It features five dancers wearing distinct colored costumes representing the cardinal directions and the center. The dance serves both as a ritual to drive away evil spirits and a majestic display of traditional Korean court artistry.
profile.profile_long: Cheoyongmu is a storied Korean court dance rooted in the legend of Cheoyong, the son of the Dragon King Yongwang. According to tradition, Cheoyong saved his wife from a smallpox spirit by using dance and music to drive the entity away. This narrative evolved into a formal court performance, historically used during New Year’s Eve exorcism rites and royal banquets to ensure tranquility and good fortune. From the Silla period through the Goryeo dynasty, the dance was performed by a single dancer, but it eventually transitioned into a five-person performance during the Joseon era. The dancers are clad in white, blue, black, red, and yellow, symbolizing the four cardinal directions and the center, reflecting the Confucian theory of the Five Elements. Their attire is highly specific: they wear light wine-colored masks with white teeth, tin earrings, necklaces of lead beads, and black hats adorned with two peony blossoms and seven peaches—items believed to ward off malevolent forces. The movement style is characterized by majesty and vigor, shifting through various tempos and styles of music, which are punctuated by lyrical song recitations. Beyond the dance itself, the tradition encompasses the craftsmanship of mask-making and the folk belief that placing an image of Cheoyong on a house gate could repel disease. Though the dance faced a temporary disappearance following the 1910 annexation treaty, it was revived in the 1920s and remains a vital part of Korean cultural heritage, recognized by UNESCO in 2009.

sections.origins_and_history: Originating in the Unified Silla period, Cheoyongmu is the oldest surviving Korean court dance. It evolved from a solo performance into a five-person dance by the Joseon era. It was historically used for exorcism rites and royal banquets.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by five men who move with stateliness and vigor. The performance is punctuated by lyrical song recitations and varies in tempo and style.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music includes lyrical song recitations and varies in style and tempo to accompany the dancers' movements.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear costumes in yellow, red, blue, white, and black. They don light wine-colored masks with white teeth, tin earrings, lead bead necklaces, and black hats decorated with two peony blossoms and seven peaches.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a ritual to drive off evil spirits and smallpox, it was performed at royal banquets and New Year's Eve exorcisms to promote good fortune and tranquility.
sections.lineage: Derived from the legend of Cheoyong, son of the Dragon King Yongwang.
